title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
0.1 Aims
This book applies DeCovarT to the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource. It records what is run: the data, the algorithms as implemented, the hyperparameters and their values, the code, the outputs, and which outputs are stale. The reasons behind each choice are in the DeCovarT vignettes; each chapter links to the vignette section that states them and does not restate the theory.
The target is a covariance plug-in for the likelihood, not a biologically interpretable gene regulatory network (03-2, why a regularised covariance). Indices follow the article: gene g=1,\ldots,G, type j=1,\ldots,J, bulk sample i=1,\ldots,N, cell c, with C_j cells of type j.

title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
Estimate, for each labelled cell type j at each bulk-matched time, the mean \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and the within-type covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{W,j} of a gene panel, on the linear scale that DeCovarT’s convolution needs. The source is one single-specimen scRNA-seq reference (GSE229513, Section 2.1).
Choose that panel for the purpose: genes whose moments can be estimated in every type and that carry information about the proportions \boldsymbol{p} (Section 3.1).
Plug the moments into DeCovarT and deconvolve the bulk series (GSE229386) where a single-cell reference matches it: the standard-Wnt samples at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h.

0.2 Pipeline
Figure 1 lists the nine steps in the order the scripts run them. Steps 2 to 5 are Section 3.1; step 7 is Section 4.1; step 8 is 2.1, three regimes; step 9 is Section 5.1.






Figure 1: “Analysis pipeline, read left to right on each row. Row 1 builds the gene panel from the single-cell counts: quality control and a presence gate in every type (tier i), a count-model screen of the type effect ranked by deviance explained (tier ii), and a cross-platform filter (tier iii) fitted independently at each of the three matched pairs (single-cell 48 h, 72 h and 96 h against the standard-Wnt bulk at the same time). Row 2 estimates one covariance per type and time on the linear scale, with the tuning parameter of each estimator chosen by cross-validated held-out Gaussian log-likelihood, lifts the estimates to DeCovarT’s moments and deconvolves the matched bulk at all three times. The dashed box is optional; it needs the covariances of step 7.”

title: 2  Suppinger gastruloids
text:
2.1 Hierarchical design
Single-cell UMI counts and bulk HTSeq tables come from the murine gastruloid resource of Suppinger and colleagues (Cell Stem Cell, 2023; GEO GSE229513 and GSE229386; (Suppinger et al. 2023)).
The scRNA-seq experiment is one 10x Chromium 3′ v3 resource from one specimen series, not a panel of independent biological replicates. DeCovarT treats it as the one-replicate regime (2.1, one single-cell replicate). Zeros are taken as molecule-sampling counts (?nte-drop-zico). GSE250136 is a later stem-embryo dataset and is not part of this resource.
Figure 2.1 draws the two designs side by side.
Single-cell (GSE229513). The first factor is the mESC cell line (B-S or SBR), the second the time slot. Each line covers six slots, and only 48 h is profiled in both. At the three times of the bulk series the cell counts are (output/naive_marker_selection/tables/batch_by_time.csv):
Cell line is therefore confounded with time except at 48 h, and it is not a covariate in any fit of this book. The two lines are treated as one developmental trajectory (Figure 2.4). Gene ranking and covariance estimation run independently at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, the slots with a bulk time point (Section 3.3.1, Section 4.1). At 48 h the two lines are pooled; Section 3.7.1 measures what pooling changes.
Bulk RNA-seq (GSE229386). The first factor is the Wnt schedule: the standard pulse at 48 h, or an early pulse at 24 h. The second factor is the time point, 48 h, 72 h or 96 h, each with three biological replicates. No single-cell slot carries the early schedule, so the early-Wnt bulk has no single-cell counterpart at any time. The three single-cell slots used in this book instead match the three time points of the standard-Wnt bulk: single-cell 48 h (B-S and SBR pooled), 72 h (SBR) and 96 h (B-S), each against three biological replicates of the standard-Wnt bulk at that time. The cross-platform filter of Section 3.4 is therefore fitted at all three standard-Wnt time points, never on the early-Wnt arm.

2.2 Seurat processing
Embeddings, QC and clustering follow the Seurat workflow of the Suppinger resource (Suppinger et al. 2023), drawn in Figure 2.2: Alevin counts, scater QC, SCTransform Pearson residuals per batch for integration, CCA, PCA, UMAP and Louvain clustering. The deposited object (Seurat 4.1.0) holds the raw counts (RNA, 27,027 genes, 71,005 cells), the SCT layer and the integrated assay. The SCT and integrated layers keep the same 71,005 cells and only 2,944 genes: the variable features of the CCA integration, chosen over all twelve time points and both batches. Two products of that workflow are used here: the cell-type labels (celltypeannotation), and that 2,944-gene list, which was the gene allow-list of the legacy panel only; the current tier (i) starts from the raw counts and records the list for comparison (Section 3.2). The authors’ residuals themselves are not used: the ranking fits its own negative-binomial GLMs per time slot (Section 3.3.1), the legacy panel refitted SCTransform v2 per slot (legacy SCTransform fit), and the covariances are estimated from raw counts (Section 4.1.1).






Figure 2.2: Seurat workflow used to extract embeddings and downstream analyses on GSE229513.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.1 Scope and status
This chapter builds the gene panel on which the covariances of Section 4.1 are estimated. It is the application that the feature-selection vignette (3.1) leaves to this book: filters as applied, settings, rank tables and code. It runs on the single-cell counts of GSE229513 at the three bulk-matched times (Section 2.1), one time at a time. What the panel must achieve, and why each step is there, is stated in the vignette (3.1, what the genes are for): genes whose type-level moments can be estimated in every type and that carry information about \boldsymbol{p}. The sections follow the tiers of the vignette: (i) quality control and prior knowledge, (ii) cross-cell consistency and (iii) cross-platform consistency are implemented here; (iv), down-weighting by the model, is a remark: it takes place when DeCovarT itself is fitted (Section 3.5).
The Suppinger reference is the one-specimen case of that callout. It is one technical scRNA-seq experiment (Suppinger et al. 2023), and its cells are draws from one specimen, not biological replicates (Section 2.1). Every ranking statistic below is therefore computed inside that specimen: it calibrates a screen, not a population-level claim of differential expression.
The current panel (top 500 per time, 2) comes from the legacy between/within ratio (between/within ratio). Once tiers (i) to (iii) have been run, their rank replaces it as steps 3 to 5 of Figure 1, and every output of Section 4.1 has to be refitted.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
Note 3.1: ℹ️ Cells are not biological replicates



Treating the cells of one specimen as independent replicates of a population contrast is pseudoreplication: it inflates the apparent sample size and understates the standard error of every statistic computed across cells (Zimmerman et al. 2021; Squair et al. 2021; Crowell et al. 2020). A score fitted this way, or a bootstrap that resamples cells with labels fixed, measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not to new specimens. It is reported as such wherever it is used in this book (Section 4.1, Section 7.2).

3.2 Tier (i): quality control and prior knowledge
The vignette lists the quality-control rules of the reviewed methods as examples (3.1, QC). Here the authors’ quality control is taken as given, and those rules are recorded against it rather than applied again. This tier also holds what is decided without the counts: the curated markers, forced into the panel, and the presence gate.

3.2.1 Cell and gene QC as applied
The deposited object is the authors’ filtered matrix: 27,027 genes and 71,005 cells, with the same cells in the raw counts and in the SCT layer (Section 2.2). scripts/02_01_stats_quality_control.R has been run on it. Cells.

The authors’ thresholds stand. They kept cells with more than 1,800 detected genes and less than 10 % mitochondrial counts (Suppinger et al. 2023). Both cut-offs are stricter than the deMixSC examples (200 genes, 50 %), so no fixed rule of the vignette removes a cell they kept. They were computed before the mitochondrial, ribosomal and Gm genes were removed: the mitochondrial fraction needs the chrM genes. That order is an inference, not a statement of the paper. It explains why 65 scored cells fall at or below 1,800 genes on the deposited genes, and why the mitochondrial fraction cannot be recomputed: cell_mitochondrial_fraction() returns NA, not 0, when no mt- symbol is present.
Library-size outliers are recorded, not removed. 417 scored cells (239 at 48 h, 69 at 72 h, 109 at 96 h) lie beyond 3 scaled MADs of the log library size of their type (cell_qc_rules()). They pass the authors’ QC, which is taken as given.
Slot filter. keep_bulk_matched_cells() keeps cells with a time slot in {48 h, 72 h, 96 h}, a non-missing celltypeannotation and a library size above zero. The library size is the column sum of the deposited counts over all 27,027 genes; it equals 10^{\texttt{log\_umi}} of the authors’ SCTransform models, whereas the metadata column nCount_RNA does not, and is not used.
Artefacts and small types. The culture-stress labels flagged include_in_ranking = FALSE in data/dictionaries/suppinger_celltype_crosswalk.csv (Cd63+ ectoderm-like artefact, Zscan4+ artefact) are dropped. A type with fewer than min_cells = 20 cells in a slot is left out of the scores; exiting naïve pluripotency at 72 h (8 cells) is the only such case.

(b) Distribution of the log10 library size per type, types ranked by median, with the median (point), the ±3 MAD interval (bar) and the number of cells in the label. Source: scored_slots.rds, element cell_values; scripts/02_01_vis_quality_control.R.



Figure 3.1 shows the authors’ cells against the cut-offs. Every cell sits far above the deMixSC lines. The cells below the 1,800-gene line are the low tail of a single library-size–gene trend, not a separate population, and the 3-MAD flags fall at both ends of that trend.
Genes.

Bulk symbols. Every one of the 27,027 symbols appears in the bulk HTSeq gene_name column; shared_bulk_single_cell_genes() drops the 49 whose rows carry more than one Ensembl id once the version suffix is removed (element shared of scored_slots.rds). drop_mitochondrial_genes() is kept as a guard and removes nothing here.
Fractional counts. The deposited counts are Salmon/Alevin estimates. A UMI compatible with several genes is divided among them, equally when no read tells them apart, so 12.8 % of the non-zero entries are fractions such as 1/2, 1/3 or 1/4. The share is not tied to expression level; it concentrates in multi-copy loci (the protocadherin-γ cluster, processed pseudogenes, histone genes), whose counts are shares of the same UMIs as their paralogues. Their within-type correlations are then fixed by the split, not measured, which matters for the covariances of Section 4.1. The 2,178 genes whose non-zero entries are more than 90 % fractional are dropped (495 of them detected in at least 500 cells), the share being computed on all 71,005 cells without labels (fractional_count_share(); elements fractional and dropped_fractional of scored_slots.rds). The counts are not rounded: rounding would turn every 0.5 into 0. glmGamPoi accepts non-integer counts, and the negative-binomial likelihood is then a quasi-likelihood.
Presence gate. After these filters 24,816 genes enter the presence gate of Section 3.2.3 at each time; 8,643 (48 h), 8,636 (72 h) and 8,788 (96 h) pass it (element presence of scored_slots.rds).
Authors’ gene list. The 2,944 genes of the SCT layer are the CCA integration features: 3,000 anchor features, of which 56 (histone genes, MHC H2- genes, Nme2, 4930537H20Rik) are absent from the layer (element anchor_missing of scored_slots.rds). They are variable over all twelve time points and both batches, not a quality filter. Of them, 1,622 (48 h), 1,589 (72 h) and 1,562 (96 h) also pass the filters above, which pass 7,021, 7,047 and 7,226 genes outside the list. The list was the gene set of the legacy panel only (legacy panel).

3.2.2 Knowledge-driven markers
Curated markers are hard prior knowledge: they are united with the ranked panel at each time whatever their score, so they are chosen without the counts and cannot be a product of the rank. The list is short: data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv, with columns cell_type_excel (lineage on the signalling map), cell_type_suppinger (the matching Suppinger label, or NA) and gene_marker. Symbols are mapped offline with org.Mm.eg.db (R/02_01_stats_quality_control.R), not biomaRt. The lineage groups of the same file are the gene modules of the tier (iii) filter (1).
Fifteen of the 19 mouse symbols are in the 2,944-gene allow-list. Under a uniform draw of 19 genes from the 27,027 RNA symbols the expected overlap is about 2.1; the hypergeometric upper tail is P(X\ge 15)=8.8\times10^{-12} (marker_sct_hypergeometric.csv). The four absent markers are Myod1, Pax6, Sox1 and Tfap2a (venn_markers_vs_counts.pdf).


3.2.3 Presence gate
A gene enters the ranking at a given time only if it is detected, and varies, in every scored type at that time. With \delta_{gj} the fraction of cells of type j with a non-zero count for gene g, and v_{gj} the within-type variance of the counts,

\min_{j}\delta_{gj}\ge\delta_{\min}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\min_{j}v_{gj}>0 .
\tag{3.1}
presence_gate() in R/02_01_stats_quality_control.R returns one row per gene with min_detection, min_variance and a logical pass that applies both conditions; \delta_{\min} is the argument min_frac, fixed at 0.05 before the ranks are seen (the default and the value of every call below). The reasons for a gate in every type, rather than in at least one, are in 3.1, presence. In the current outputs the gate is absent. Its absence is one cause of the constant-gene fallback of the covariance estimates (Section 4.1).
Projections of the gated genes. Figure 3.3 projects the scored cells of each slot on the genes that pass the gate. They are descriptive, not a selection rule.

Input. The analytic Pearson residuals of the null model M_0 of Equation 3.2 (intercept and library-size offset, gene-wise negative-binomial overdispersion, pearson_residuals_m0()), the variance-stabilised scale of the tier (ii) count model, without SCTransform and without clipping. Genes are centred, not scaled: the residuals are already on a common scale, and scaling would up-weight genes that carry mostly noise. PLS-DA (mixOmics::plsda(), two components, cell type as response) uses the same matrix. The shifted logarithm \log(1+x/s_c), centred and scaled, remains available (input = "shifted_log").
Small first axes. The first two principal components explain together 1.3 % (72 h) to 3.1 % (48 h) of the variance: the type structure is spread over many genes.
Cell line at 48 h. The epiblast, the large type at 48 h, splits into two clouds, and the panels coloured by cell line show that the split is the cell line. The sign of the first principal component puts 5,301 of the 5,470 B-S (batch 1) epiblast cells on one side and 5,081 of the 5,120 SBR (batch 2) cells on the other (projection_pc1_by_batch.csv). Even the PLS-DA, fitted to separate the types, separates the two lines on its second component. Cell line is therefore the main source of variation within that type, which is why the labels of tier (ii) are permuted within batch (Section 3.3.2).

The PLS-DA components put the rare types (naïve and ectopic pluripotency, gut) at the ends of the axes.

title: 3  Feature selection
text:
3.3 Tier (ii): cross-cell consistency
A gene is kept when its counts separate the scored types consistently across the cells of one slot. The theory, and the comparison of the four tests, are in 3.1, cross-cell consistency.

3.3.1 Count-model fit per time
At each of 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, on the genes that pass the presence gate and the cells of the scored types, two negative-binomial GLMs are fitted gene by gene with glmGamPoi::glm_gp() (Ahlmann-Eltze and Huber 2020):

\begin{aligned}
M_0:\quad \log m_{gc} &= \beta_{0g}+\log s_{c},\\
M_1:\quad \log m_{gc} &= \beta_{0g}+\beta_{g,j(c)}+\log s_{c},
\end{aligned}
\qquad
x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{NB}(m_{gc},\psi_{g}),\quad
\operatorname{Var}x_{gc}=m_{gc}+m_{gc}^{2}/\psi_{g},
\tag{3.2}
with s_c the size factor of cell c (full RNA library size, the column sum of the deposited counts, divided by its median), passed as offset = log(s_c) with size_factors = 1 so that it is not applied twice. glmGamPoi reports the overdispersion 1/\psi_g. For the likelihood-ratio statistic \psi_g is the gene-wise maximum-likelihood estimate under M_1 and M_0 is refitted at the same \psi_g; for the quasi-likelihood test it is shrunk across genes (Section 3.3.2). Cell type and nothing else is a covariate; cell line is not (Section 2.1).
The ranking statistic is the cell-weighted deviance explained,

R^{2}_{D,g}=1-\frac{\mathcal{D}_g(M_1)}{\mathcal{D}_g(M_0)},
\qquad
\Lambda_g=\mathcal{D}_g(M_0)-\mathcal{D}_g(M_1),
\tag{3.3}
with both deviances summed over every cell at the same \psi_g, so that \Lambda_g is the likelihood-ratio statistic of the type effect. Each cell has weight one, which is the weighting of the likelihood itself; the type-equal weighting of the legacy rank (Equation 3.7) is not carried over.
Why SCTransform is not needed. SCTransform fits the same M_0 (Hafemeister and Satija 2019; Choudhary and Satija 2022), but with two departures that matter for a screen of the type effect:

its overdispersion is regularised across genes, as a smooth function of the mean, so a gene whose spread departs from the trend (for example a marker that is bimodal across types) gets the wrong residual scale;
its Pearson residuals are clipped at \pm\sqrt{n/30}, n the cells of the fit (Table 3.7). Under M_0, which has no type term, the cells of a rare type that expresses a marker, and the cells of a highly expressed gene, have the largest residuals: they carry the type signal. Clipping shrinks exactly these high-leverage cells.

Here \psi_g is estimated gene by gene and nothing is clipped. The SCTransform Pearson residual r^{P}_{gc}=(x_{gc}-\hat m_{gc})/\sqrt{V(\hat m_{gc})} is also not standardised. The standardised residual divides it by \sqrt{\hat\varphi(1-h_{gc})}, with \hat\varphi the dispersion scale (1 for the NB likelihood) and h_{gc} the leverage of cell c (Section 3.4.1). The vignette states the model and the residuals (3.1, count null model and Pearson residuals).

compare_type_effect_tests() (R/02_02_stats_cross_cell.R) computes four tests of the joint type effect (J-1 degrees of freedom) per gene, on the fits of Equation 3.2. They answer one question with different reference laws; the vignette compares their assumptions (3.1, four tests).

The permutation follows Freedman and Lane (Freedman and Lane 1983): the reduced model is M_0, whose fitted part carries no type information, so permuting its residuals against fixed labels is the same as permuting the labels. Welch’s G is used because it stays pivotal when the within-type variances differ, as recommended by Winkler et al. (2014). One permutation of the C labels is drawn and applied to every gene, B times, and p_g=(1+\#\{G^{*}_g\ge G_g\})/(B+1). B is fixed before the run (the code default is 2,000). Its floor 1/(B+1)\approx5\times10^{-4} limits both the resolution of a gate on this test and Kendall’s \tau, since genes at the floor are tied (3.1, calibration).
Permutations within batch. At 48 h the slot pools the two cell lines, which are the two batches of the object (B-S in batch 1, SBR in batch 2), and the type mix differs between them. An unrestricted permutation would then read a cell-line shift as a type effect. Labels are therefore permuted within batch (strata = batch), which keeps the type counts of each batch; at 72 h and 96 h each slot holds one batch, so the restriction changes nothing there. Cell line is still not a covariate of M_0 or M_1.
Gate and rank. One test is chosen before the ranks are seen and used as a Benjamini–Hochberg gate over the genes that pass the presence gate. The gate is the permuted Welch G (gate_test = "welch_perm", the default of rank_genes_omnibus()): in the simulation of the vignette it is the only test that keeps the false discovery rate at its nominal level when the within-type variances differ (0.05, against 0.16 to 0.21 for the other tests compared there), at the cost of power (0.41, against 0.76 to 0.85) (3.1, four tests). Every gene that passes the gate enters the panel; no cap is imposed (n_select = Inf). The cap of 500 genes per time was inherited from the legacy panel and had no data-driven justification. The genes that pass are still ranked by R^{2}_{D,g} (Equation 3.3), ties broken by \Lambda_g, to order and report them. Why a gate followed by an effect size, rather than a rank by p-value, is in the vignette (link above).
The gate controls false discoveries, not relevance. With thousands of cells, a type effect of any size passes Benjamini–Hochberg, so the panel contains genes whose effect is real but small. No effect-size floor is added: their weight is left to the model, through the covariances that DeCovarT estimates and inverts (tier (iv), Section 3.5).
Multiplicity. A permutation p-value is marginal: one per gene. The gate is applied to every gene that passes the presence gate, so a correction across genes is still needed, and Benjamini–Hochberg at 0.05 is applied to the permutation p-values of each slot. A false discovery rate suits a screen whose output is then ranked by an effect size; a family-wise rate (for example a max-T adjustment from the same permutations) would discard genes that the rank needs. Three consequences of the permutation scale are reported with the outputs (permutation_floor.csv):

with m genes tested, all the genes at the floor 1/(B+1) pass only when there are at least m/\{0.05\,(B+1)\} of them, about m/100 for B=2{,}000;
near the Benjamini–Hochberg cut, the Monte Carlo standard error of a p-value is \sqrt{p(1-p)/B}, so a gene close to the cut can move across it with another seed;
each slot is gated at 0.05 on its own. The union over the three slots, which feeds tier (iii), has no single false discovery rate; a Benjamini–Hochberg over the pooled (gene, slot) p-values would give one.

Calibration. Under one within-batch permutation of the labels (Figure 3.4), the analytic tests are anti-conservative at 48 h: at the 0.01 level the likelihood ratio rejects 2.9 times the nominal rate, the quasi-likelihood F 2.8 times and the shifted-log ANOVA 3.4 times. A within-batch permutation keeps the association between type and cell line, and these tests do not model the cell line, so its effect reads as a type effect. The permuted Welch G rejects 0.63 times the nominal rate there. At 72 h and 96 h, one batch each, every test is at or below its nominal rate except the ANOVA (1.2 to 1.4 times at 0.01).
Gate. The permuted Welch G passes 1,417 (48 h), 3,420 (72 h) and 5,821 (96 h) of the 8,643, 8,636 and 8,788 tested genes at BH 0.05. The genes at the floor 1/(B+1) (635, 1,686 and 2,869) far exceed the about 87 needed for all of them to pass (permutation_floor.csv), so the floor does not limit the gate.
Agreement. Kendall’s \tau between the likelihood ratio and the quasi-likelihood F is 0.98 at every time; between the permuted Welch G and the other three it is 0.68 to 0.80 (Figure 3.5).
Panel. Every gated gene enters the panel (Figure 3.6): 1,417, 3,420 and 5,821 genes at 48, 72 and 96 h, 6,604 across the three times (selected_<time>.csv, ordered by R^{2}_{D}). The largest R^{2}_{D} is 0.60 (Slc2a3 at 96 h), but 99 % (48 h), 96 % (72 h) and 89 % (96 h) of the gated genes explain less than 5 % of the deviance (median R^{2}_{D} 0.003, 0.005 and 0.010): real but small effects, whose weight is the relevance question left to the model (tier (iv)).
Overdispersion. The gene-wise 1/\psi_g decreases with the mean (Figure 3.7); a group of genes sits near zero, the Poisson limit of the fit.

3.4 Tier (iii): cross-platform consistency
This tier compares the bulk with the single-cell reference, so it needs a matched bulk (Figure 2.1). It removes genes whose bulk expression the reference cannot produce. The approaches reviewed, the model behind the statistic and its identifiability are in 3.1, cross-platform consistency; the comparison table of second-generation methods is in 3.1, review table.

3.4.1 Outlier cells and genes
Two fits are diagnosed with Cook’s distance, which combines leverage and residual (3.1, leverage and influence).

Cells, in the M_1 fit of each gene (Equation 3.2). cook_cells() uses the IRLS weight w_{gc}=m_{gc}^{2}/V(m_{gc}); in a one-way design the leverage is h_{gc}=w_{gc}/\sum_{c'\in j(c)}w_{gc'}, so a cell of the 29-cell somite differentiation front has a leverage near 1/29 and an epiblast cell near 1/10{,}590. Cook’s distance is r^{P\,2}_{gc}h_{gc}/\{J(1-h_{gc})^{2}\} with dispersion scale 1.
Genes, in the weighted regression of each bulk replicate on the reference signature, across genes. cook_genes() takes the composition and the final weights of the plug-in fit

and computes the hat values on the types with a positive coefficient.


A cell or a gene is flagged only when its leverage and its standardised residual are both large (defaults: leverage above three times its mean, J/C for cells and J/G for genes, and |r^{SP}|>3). High leverage alone marks a rare type or a highly expressed marker, which carries information; a large residual alone marks an ordinary tail count. Nothing is clipped or down-weighted: flagged cells and genes are listed with their type and counts, and whether to drop one is decided by reading that list.

3.4.2 Bulk consistency filter
The filter needs a single-cell slot and a bulk sample of the same condition.

Matched pairs. The single-cell reference matches the standard-Wnt bulk at all three times used in this book: single-cell 48 h (B-S and SBR pooled), 72 h (SBR) and 96 h (B-S), each against three biological replicates of the standard-Wnt bulk at that time.
No match for early Wnt. The early-Wnt bulk (Wnt pulse at 24 h) has no single-cell counterpart at any time, so no bulk–reference comparison is possible on that arm.
Fit. At each of the three matched times independently, in two steps. First, a \boldsymbol{p}-free check: the distance of each normalised bulk value to the range of the type means, with RNA-Sieve’s range bound and median-absolute-deviation outlier rule (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021) (bulk_consistency_filter(), a heuristic). Second, the tail statements below, on a statistic that uses a plug-in composition.
Apply (planned, not applied). The rule was to remove a gene flagged at any of the three matched times from the panel at every time, including the early-Wnt arm. The run below shows that the model-based statements flag 93 to 95 % of the panel under A3, and still 70 to 72 % after a cross-fitted gene-wise platform ratio, so the rule is not applied (see Results).
Drift across times. With three matched times the flags can be compared across 48 h, 72 h and 96 h. platform_drift_summary() classifies each gene by the times at which it is flagged (T4 by default) and by the sign of its standardised discrepancy D_{gi}/\operatorname{sd}D_{gi}: flagged at several times with one sign supports treating the platform effect as a property of the gene; flagged at one time only does not.
Code. Tier (iii) has two files: R/02_03_stats_influence.R (Cook’s distance for cells and genes, Section 3.4.1) and R/02_03_stats_tail_bounds.R (range check, plug-in, tail statements, quantile band, drift, transcript length and the gene-wise platform ratio). scripts/02_03_stats_cross_platform_consistency.R runs both. It has been run; its outputs in output/feature_selection/tier_03/ are tail_order_<time>.csv (A3), platform_drift.csv (flagged genes only), platform_log_ratio.csv, platform_length.csv, platform_ratio.csv (cross-fitted \log_2\hat b_g and its standard error, per held-out time and method), a3_shift_summary.csv (one row per time and variant), settings.csv and cross_platform.rds (every table, tracked with DVC). The figures are drawn by scripts/02_03_vis_cross_platform.R.

Plug-in composition: deMixSC, not plain NNLS. For each bulk replicate i, plugin_composition_demixsc() fits the bulk counts y_{gi} on the per-cell type means of the reference by iterated weighted non-negative least squares, as deMixSC does: weights 1/(\hat y_{gi}^{2}+(y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2}+c) with c=2. Plain NNLS is not used as a plug-in, for two reasons.

Weights of the model. Under DeCovarT the variance of a bulk count is gene-specific and depends on \boldsymbol{p} and on the type means. Unweighted NNLS gives every gene the same weight, so the most expressed genes decide \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}. The deMixSC weights are inverse-variance weights that follow the current fit: the diagonal, plug-in counterpart of the generalised least squares that DeCovarT solves (Section 5.1). Of the two, it is the closer to the final model.
Robustness to the genes under test. The residual term (y_{gi}-\hat y_{gi})^{2} down-weights the genes that the bulk expresses far from the reference, which are the genes this filter must find, so that they do not bias \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} and, in turn, their own statistic.

Non-negative least squares remains only the solver of each reweighting step (nnls::nnls(), the Lawson–Hanson algorithm). deMixSC also calibrates a gene set G2 on a same-aliquot benchmark; none exists for Suppinger, so G2 is empty. a_i is the sum of the coefficients and \hat p_{ji} the coefficients divided by a_i; the extra overdispersion between platforms is fixed at 1. MuSiC (Wang et al. 2019) is not used, because its weights need at least two donors. What the plug-in costs is in 3.1, plug-in.

Statistic. With \hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} the mean raw count per cell of type j over its C_j reference cells, and \hat\psi_{gj} the negative-binomial size matched to their mean and variance (type_moments_nb(); raw counts, because a bulk is a sum of raw cell profiles),

\qquad

\tag{3.4}
for a gene g and a module M; \operatorname{sd}D_{gi} is the negative-binomial standard deviation with n_i=a_i bulk cells.

Modules. The lineage groups (cell_type_excel) of the signalling dictionary of Section 3.2.2. They were written before any count was seen, so the module flags are not circular. Each group has at most four genes, and a module with fewer than two panel genes is skipped.
Dependency graph. Inside a module, module_dependency_graph() joins the gene pairs with the largest within-type correlations, with maximum degree \le10 and mean degree \le3. With at most four genes both caps are met by construction. Genes without an edge are assumed independent; T2 uses the within-type correlations on the edges, T5 only the colouring of the graph (greedy_colouring()).
Quantile band. quantile_band_flags() regresses y_{gi}/a_i on \sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} across the genes of one replicate, at \tau=0.01 and 0.99, without a count model. Each bound above bounds a quantile of D_{gi} under a model; the band estimates it from the genes, assuming they are exchangeable given the fitted value (3.1, comparison of the bounds).
Ranking on the simulated tails. The vignette compares the statements on one gene and one module, which is not a Suppinger result (3.1, thresholds; gene tails; module tails). Per gene, T4 has the largest threshold and does not under-cover. Per module, T5 has the largest threshold and does not under-cover. T3 is far too small for a high-expression gene.
Multiplicity, two counts. The level 0.01 per tail is per gene. In the vignette, that level flags about 60 consistent genes out of about 3,000: that count is the vignette’s one comparison. Here, the Suppinger panel is 6,615 genes times three replicates, which would give about 200 (gene, replicate) flags per tail and statement if the model held. The run flags about 6,200 genes (below).

Results. The panel is the 6,604 genes that pass the tier (ii) gate at any time, united with the mapped markers: 6,616 genes, of which 6,615 are in each slot. All three variants below run on that panel.

What the tail statements assume. Every statement T1 to T5 tests D_{gi} against its spread under assumption A3: each gene has the same mean count per cell in the bulk as in the reference, so the bulk differs from a_i\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj} only by the negative-binomial sampling of a_i cells. With a_i\approx1{,}200 to 1{,}900 cells that sampling averages out, so \operatorname{sd}D_{gi} is small, and a gene is flagged when D_{gi} is more than about 2.3 of these standard deviations from 0 (T1; the Chernoff statements are somewhat wider).
What the data show under A3. The median |D_{gi}|/\operatorname{sd}D_{gi} is 17 at every time: the discrepancies are about 17 times larger, and their variance about 300 times larger, than A3 allows; 91 to 92 % of the (gene, replicate) values lie beyond \pm2.33, where 2 % are expected (Figure 3.9). T4, the most conservative per gene, flags 6,147 (48 h), 6,220 (72 h) and 6,274 (96 h) of the 6,615 genes (a3_shift_summary.csv, Figure 3.11). These flags measure the failure of A3, not a defect of individual genes.
The discrepancy is a gene-wise ratio. For each gene and time, the mean over replicates of \log_2\{(y_{gi}/a_i)/\sum_j\hat
p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj}\} (platform_log_ratio()) has an interquartile range of 2.0 to 2.2 across genes: half the genes are more than 2-fold away from the reference (platform_log_ratio.csv). The same genes are off in the same direction at every time: the Spearman correlation of the ratios is 0.97 (48 h–72 h), 0.95 (72 h–96 h) and 0.94 (48 h–96 h) (Figure 3.12). 5,890 genes are flagged by T4 at two or three times with one sign; the 466 flagged with a sign change and the 226 flagged at one time only sit near a ratio of 0, where a small difference flips the sign or the flag.
The ratio follows transcript length. The bulk is a full-length library and the reference a 3′ UMI library (protocols below), so a gene’s bulk reads grow with its transcript length and its reference counts do not. The prediction is a slope of 1 of the log2 ratio on log2 length. The median-regression slope is 1.06 (48 h, 95 % gene-bootstrap interval 1.02 to 1.10), 1.18 (72 h, 1.13 to 1.22) and 1.06 (96 h, 1.01 to 1.10); Spearman’s correlation is 0.55 to 0.59, and a loess on length explains 31 to 34 % of the variance of the ratio (platform_length.csv, Figure 3.8). Length is a large part of the platform effect, but two thirds of the gene-to-gene variation remain. The bootstrap treats genes as independent, so the intervals are too narrow if genes are correlated.
Dividing by a cross-fitted ratio. With the free gene-wise ratio (estimated on the two other times), the interquartile range of the residual log2 ratio falls from 2.0–2.2 to 0.38–0.42, the share of genes more than 2-fold off from 51–54 % to 2–4 %, and the range rule flags 79, 309 and 82 genes instead of 3,179, 3,802 and 2,859 (Figure 3.10, Figure 3.11). The ratio learnt at 72 and 96 h (primitive streak, mesoderm) transfers to the epiblast bulk at 48 h, and conversely, so for most genes the effect belongs to the gene, not to a type. The length-only ratio removes less: residual interquartile range 1.5 to 1.6, range flags 2,007 to 2,940.
A residual remains. With the gene-wise ratio the median |z| is 2.0 to 2.2, and 44 to 48 % of the values lie beyond \pm2.33 instead of 2 %; T4 still flags 4,628, 4,751 and 4,722 genes (Figure 3.9). The residual log ratio (interquartile range about 0.4 in log2 units, a 30 % spread) is far larger than both the negative-binomial sampling of the bulk and the uncertainty of the ratio itself (median standard error of \log_2\hat b_g 0.06 to 0.07, platform_ratio.csv). Three sources are possible, none tested here: a ratio that depends on the type as well as the gene, which is not identified without paired measurements; biological differences between the gastruloids profiled in bulk and in single cell, which are different specimens; and errors of the plug-in composition. Our reading is that the tail statements need an extra between-platform overdispersion, fixed at 1 (none) here, before their flags can single out genes.
Two side effects. The MAD rules flag more genes with the ratio (587 to 720 against 299 to 463), because one of their summaries is a bulk-to-reference ratio. The model-free quantile band flags 191 to 203 genes with the ratio and 154 to 161 under A3, 2.3 to 3.1 % of the panel, near the 2 % it is fitted for. The residual log ratios are negatively correlated between times (Spearman −0.25 to −0.45): this is built in by cross-fitting, since each time’s ratio is the average of the two others, and is not a drift.
Plug-in composition. Under A3, epiblast takes all of the 48 h bulk and the primitive streak all of the 72 h bulk (shares of at least 0.999), the types that dominate the reference (97 % and 93 % of the scored cells); at 96 h pre-somitic mesoderm takes 0.73 and caudal mesoderm 0.26. With the gene-wise ratio, the 48 h bulk becomes 0.91 epiblast and 0.08 exiting naïve pluripotency, 72 h is unchanged (0.99 primitive streak), and the 96 h composition inverts: caudal mesoderm 0.72, pre-somitic mesoderm 0.25 (Figure 3.13). The ratio used at 96 h was learnt at 48 and 72 h, where neither mesoderm type exists, so the genes that separate the two types carry ratios estimated from other cell states. No ground truth exists for these bulk samples: the inversion shows that the plug-in composition is not robust to the platform model, not which composition is right.
Cook’s distance. No gene is flagged in the weighted bulk fit at any time. This is a property of the deMixSC weights, not a finding: with w_g=1/(\hat y_g^{2}+e_g^{2}+c), \sqrt{w_g}\,|e_g|<1, so the standardised residual is bounded (it stays within \pm1.7) and never reaches 3. Among cells, 21,686 to 27,679 (gene, cell) pairs are flagged per time, all in the small types, where a cell’s leverage can exceed 3J/C (Figure 3.14).

Gene-wise platform ratio: method. The two libraries differ by design. The bulk (GSE229386) is an Illumina Stranded mRNA Ligation library of poly(A) RNA, aligned with STAR and counted with HTSeq on GENCODE vM24 (mm10); the reference (GSE229513) is 10x Genomics Single Cell 3′ v3, quantified with Salmon/Alevin on GENCODE M24 (GRCm38) (GEO series records). Full-length single-cell protocols show the length bias of bulk RNA-seq and UMI protocols do not TODO-cite: Phipson, Zappia & Oshlack 2017, Gene length and detection bias in single cell RNA sequencing protocols, F1000Research 6:595, doi:10.12688/f1000research.11290.1; the bulk side is the transcript-length bias of RNA-seq counts TODO-cite: Oshlack & Wakefield 2009, Transcript length bias in RNA-seq data confounds systems biology, Biology Direct 4:14, doi:10.1186/1745-6150-4-14. The model, its identifiability conditions and the tail statements with a plug-in ratio are in 3.1, plug-in platform ratio. As applied here:

Length. gene_transcript_length() averages the exonic length of the UCSC knownGene transcripts of each gene (TxDb.Mmusculus.UCSC.mm10.knownGene 3.10.0, GenomicFeatures::transcriptLengths()), matched by Ensembl id through org.Mm.eg.db, then by symbol: 6,564 genes by Ensembl id, 24 by symbol, 28 without a length. That annotation is based on GENCODE VM23, one release before the authors’ vM24. Adapted from annotate_genes_local() of GastroDeconv2FateMap, which uses the genomic span instead (introns included).
Three variants, no filtering. (i) A3, no ratio. (ii) A ratio from length: a robust loess of the per-gene median log ratio on log2 length. (iii) A free gene-wise ratio: the deMixSC plug-in on y_{gi}/\hat b_g alternates with \log\hat b_g= median over the pooled replicates of the log ratio, until the largest change is below 10^{-3} (18 to 21 rounds; estimate_platform_ratio()). In (ii) and

\operatorname{median}_g\log\hat b_g=0, since a_i absorbs a common factor.

Cross-fitting. The ratio used at one time is estimated on the six replicates of the two other times (cross_fit_platform_ratio()), so it cannot absorb the residual it is meant to test, and its transfer across compositions is what is tested.
Statistic. bulk_tail_filter(platform_ratio, platform_var) divides the bulk by \hat b_g before the plug-in fit, and adds the delta-method term (\sum_j\hat p_{ji}\hat{\tilde\mu}_{gj})^{2}\operatorname{Var}\log\hat b_g to the variance of D_{gi} in z and in T1; T1-log, T3, T4 and the module statements treat \hat b_g as known. The RNA-Sieve range and MAD rules need no composition and run on y_{gi}/\hat b_g as well.

What this changes: no gene is removed at this tier. A cross-fitted gene-wise ratio removes most of the platform shift, so it belongs in the model of tier (iv) rather than in a filter; the tail statements become usable as a filter only once a between-platform overdispersion is added for what the ratio leaves.






Figure 3.8: Platform ratio against transcript length. Per time, the log2 ratio of bulk per cell to the fitted reference under A3, one value per panel gene (mean over three replicates), against the log2 mean transcript length (exonic, UCSC knownGene mm10, averaged over isoforms), as 2D bins with counts on a log scale. Orange: median regression; dashed: line of slope 1 through the medians, the prediction for a full-length bulk against 3′ UMI counts. The label gives the slope with its gene-bootstrap 95 % interval (1,000 resamples), Spearman’s correlation and the share of variance explained by a loess. Source: cross_platform.rds, elements log_ratio, lengths and length_test; scripts/02_03_vis_cross_platform.R.

Signed \log_{10}(1+|z|) axis; grey band: |z|\le2.33, the T1 threshold at 0.01 per tail. The label gives the share of values beyond the band. Source: cross_platform.rds, element variants.

The label gives the median absolute \log_{10} ratio. Source: cross_platform.rds, element variants.

Source: cross_platform.rds, element variants; a3_shift_summary.csv.

Dashed line: identity; under A3 the points would gather at (0, 0). Panel titles give the Spearman correlation. Source: cross_platform.rds, elements log_ratio and drift.

(a) Leverage (log scale) against standardised residual of each panel gene in the weighted bulk-on-reference fit under A3, three replicates per time; dashed lines at \pm3; no gene is flagged. (b) (Gene, cell) pairs flagged in the M_1 fits (leverage above three times its mean and |r|>3) per cell of each type and time, types ranked; labels give the number of pairs, axis labels the number of cells. Source: cross_platform.rds, elements outlier_genes and outlier_cells.



Outputs. At each time: the genes and modules flagged by each statement; their overlap (pairwise Jaccard indices and an UpSet-style table of membership patterns, tail_flag_overlap()); and the order of the statements from the most to the least conservative, read from the number of flags and the median thresholds, not assumed. # Not run. sc[[tm]]: raw counts (genes x cells) of the scored cells of
# slot tm, with labels cell_type[[tm]] and full library sizes lib[[tm]];
# bulk[[tm]]: the three standard-Wnt replicates at tm from GSE229386
# (raw counts, genes x samples), same gene identifiers; panel: genes
# selected by tier (ii) and the markers of tier (i).
source("R/02_00_utils.R")
source("R/02_01_stats_quality_control.R")
source("R/02_03_stats_tail_bounds.R")

# Step 1: p-free range check (RNA-Sieve range bound and MAD rule).
range_flags <- lapply(times, function(tm) {
  x <- sc[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE]
  ct <- droplevels(factor(cell_type[[tm]]))
  norm <- sweep(as.matrix(x), 2L, sf[[tm]], "/")
  mu <- sapply(levels(ct), function(k) rowMeans(norm[, ct == k, drop = FALSE]))
  sd <- sapply(levels(ct), function(k) apply(norm[, ct == k, drop = FALSE], 1L, stats::sd))
  out <- bulk_consistency_filter(
    bulk = bulk[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE],
    mu = mu,
    sd = sd,
    n_cells = table(ct)[levels(ct)],
    z_range = 3,
    mad_k = 3
  )
  out$gene[!out$keep]
})

# Step 2: tail statements per gene and per module, and the quantile band.
dict <- utils::read.csv("data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv")
map <- map_marker_symbols(dict$gene_marker, universe = rownames(sc[["48h"]]))
dict$gene <- map$mouse_symbol[match(dict$gene_marker, map$gene_marker)]
modules <- lapply(
  split(dict$gene, dict$cell_type_excel),
  function(g) unique(stats::na.omit(g))
)
tail_res <- lapply(times, function(tm) {
  bulk_tail_filter(
    bulk = bulk[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE],
    counts = sc[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE],
    cell_type = cell_type[[tm]],
    modules = modules,
    level = 0.01,
    c_reg = 2,
    max_degree = 10L,
    mean_degree = 3,
    min_abs_cor = 0.1
  )
})
names(tail_res) <- times
overlap <- lapply(tail_res, function(r) tail_flag_overlap(r$gene, band = r$quantile_band))

# Step 3: drift of the discrepancy across the three matched times.
drift <- platform_drift_summary(lapply(tail_res, function(r) r$gene), statement = "T4")

# Step 4: does the bulk / reference ratio follow transcript length?
# ensembl[panel]: Ensembl ids of the panel genes (bulk row names).
log_ratio <- platform_log_ratio(tail_res)
lengths <- gene_transcript_length(panel, ensembl[panel])
log2_length <- setNames(log2(lengths$mean_tx_length), lengths$gene)
length_test <- platform_length_test(log_ratio$log_ratio, log2_length, seed = 20261109L)

# Step 5: cross-fitted platform ratio (each time from the two others),
# then the same statements on bulk / b. No gene is removed.
mu_list <- lapply(tail_res, function(r) r$moments$mu)
ratio_gene <- cross_fit_platform_ratio(bulk, mu_list, method = "gene", n_iter = 30L)
ratio_length <- cross_fit_platform_ratio(
  bulk, mu_list, method = "length", log2_length = log2_length, n_iter = 30L
)
tail_gene <- lapply(times, function(tm) {
  r <- ratio_gene[[tm]]
  bulk_tail_filter(
    bulk = bulk[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE],
    counts = sc[[tm]][panel, , drop = FALSE],
    cell_type = cell_type[[tm]],
    modules = modules,
    platform_ratio = setNames(exp(r$log_b), r$gene),
    platform_var = setNames(r$var_log_b, r$gene)
  )
})

3.5 Tier (iv): down-weighting by the model
Tier (iv) is a remark, not a step of this chapter. Tiers (i) to (iii) keep or drop a gene; tier (iv) keeps every gene of the exported panel and lets the model weight it, so that genes with a large or poorly estimated within-type covariance count less in the generalised least squares of DeCovarT. That weighting happens only when DeCovarT itself is fitted on the panel of 2, with the covariances estimated in Section 4.1, in the deconvolution of Section 5.1. No gene is selected and no code runs here. Why weighting can replace a hard filter is in 3.1, down-weighting.

3.7 Perspectives

3.7.1 Cell-line sensitivity at 48 h
The reference has one specimen per slot, so cross-sample consistency (3.1, cross-sample) cannot be tested. The closest available analogue is the two cell lines at 48 h, the only slot that contains both. It is not part of the main results. The script output/naive_marker_selection/cell_line_48h/01_03_sensitivity_48h_cell_line.R refits the legacy v2 model inside B-S and inside SBR and compares the equal-cell top 500 and the per-type top 50. (It lives under output/ next to its results; scripts/01_03_export_equal_type_seurat.R is a different script.)

The two global lists share 308 of 500 genes (Jaccard 0.45).
Epiblast shares 29, and exiting naïve pluripotency 30, of its top 50.
Naïve pluripotency is scored in SBR only: B-S has fewer than 20 cells of that type.

Outputs: overlap_48h_cell_line.csv, ranks_global_48h_by_line.csv, ranks_per_cell_type_48h_by_line.csv, venn_48h_cell_line.pdf.


3.7.2 Comparison with classifier-based marker selection
A second check of the panel uses classifiers of the cell type, each inside stability selection (Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010), as in S6, sparse classifiers:

penalised multinomial logistic regression (glmnet, grouped lasso across types);
sparse PLS discriminant analysis (mixOmics::splsda());
random forest (ranger, impurity importance).

TODO-cite: glmnet (Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani 2010); mixOmics (Rohart et al. 2017); ranger (Wright & Ziegler 2017)
classifier_markers() (R/02_05_classifiers.R) subsamples half of the cells of each type 100 times, keeps the top 50 genes of each fit, and reports each gene’s selection frequency; the stable set is the genes selected in at least 60 % of the subsamples. The cells come from one specimen, so the resampling unit is the cell and the frequencies measure generalisation to new cells of this specimen (Note 3.1). The purpose is to check that the panel is biologically meaningful, robust and able to discriminate the types, not to replace it: the stable sets are compared with the omnibus panel through their overlaps (set_overlap() in R/02_00_utils.R).

3.7.3 Optional multivariate refinement
A univariate rank ignores redundancy between genes and the covariances DeCovarT models. The optional stage searches subsets of the panel with a multi-objective criterion on all types jointly (3.1, covariance-driven (post hoc) selection). It needs \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}, so it runs after Section 4.1, and it is drawn dashed in Figure 1. Its panels fall under the circularity warning of the vignette (3.1, circularity): a comparison with other methods also reports the panel of 2, chosen without the model.
Shortlist. The multi-donor pipeline of the screening appendix (S6, multi-donor pipeline) feeds NSGA-II with a DESeq2 pseudo-bulk shortlist. With one specimen, as for the Suppinger reference, the DESeq2 step does not apply, and strategy B of that appendix (presence gate, omnibus gate, effect-size rank; Section 3.2.3 and Section 3.3.2) replaces the shortlist.
Types with few cells. A joint test or objective on the panel \mathcal{G} uses the within-type covariance, which is high-dimensional when C_j is not much larger than |\mathcal{G}| (3.1, multivariate tests). With the gated panel of 2 (1,417, 3,420 and 5,821 genes at 48, 72 and 96 h), nine of the eleven scored type × time cells of Table 3.2 have C_j<|\mathcal{G}|, so their sample covariance is singular (Table 4.3):

48 h: exiting naïve pluripotency (265 cells), naïve pluripotency (36);
72 h: ectopic pluripotency (266), naïve pluripotency (66);
96 h: pre-somitic mesoderm (3,589), caudal mesoderm (1,061), gut (140), ectopic pluripotency (116), somite differentiation front (29).

Only 48 h epiblast and 72 h primitive streak have more cells than genes. For these types the objectives below use the regularised \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of Section 4.1, never the sample covariance.
Planned settings:

Optimiser. NSGA-II through mco::nsga2() (Mersmann et al. 2020). Genes are encoded as a mask in [0,1]^{G}, thresholded to a target panel size.
Objectives, all minimised:

the 2-norm condition number \kappa_{2}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\mathcal{G}}) of the mean signature restricted to the panel;
the mean pairwise MixSim overlap of the J Gaussians \mathcal{N}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}) (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021);
optionally, minus the smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information for \boldsymbol{p}, as a sensitivity objective on a shortlist of non-dominated panels.

Output. The whole Pareto front, not one panel. With one specimen, any panel chosen here is fitted on this atlas and has to be challenged on an external gastruloid cohort.

scripts/04_02_feature_selection_genetic_algorithm.R is a template: it stops with an error until the fitness function is implemented on a real panel.

# Not run. mu: G x J means; Sigma: list of J covariances (G x G), both
# on the linear scale, from the estimator selected in the covariance
# chapter.
fitness <- function(mask) {
  g <- which(mask > 0.5)
  kappa2 <- kappa(mu[g, , drop = FALSE], exact = TRUE)
  ov <- MixSim::overlap(
    Pi = rep(1 / J, J),
    Mu = t(mu[g, , drop = FALSE]),
    S = simplify2array(lapply(Sigma, \(A) A[g, g, drop = FALSE]))
  )
  c(kappa2, mean(ov$OmegaMap[upper.tri(ov$OmegaMap)]))
}
front <- mco::nsga2(fitness, idim = nrow(mu), odim = 2L,
  lower.bounds = rep(0, nrow(mu)), upper.bounds = rep(1, nrow(mu)))

Legacy panel: SCTransform ratio
The current 500-gene panel, and every covariance output of Section 4.1, come from the rank described here. It stays the source of data/intermediate/equal_type_top500_by_time.rds until the rank of tiers (ii) and (iii) has been run; it is kept as provenance of the existing files.

SCTransform v2 fit per time
rank_genes_sctransform() refits Seurat::SCTransform() separately at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (split_by = "time_point") on the allow-list genes. Cells of every non-artefact type at that time are fitted together. The fitted mean is an intercept plus a library-size offset,

\log\mu_{gc}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\log s_{c},
\qquad
x_{gc}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{gc},\psi_{g}),
\tag{3.5}
with s_{c} the full RNA library size of cell c (column sum of the unfiltered count matrix, stored as log_umi =\log_{10}s_{c}), not the sum over the allow-list. The Pearson residual is r_{gc}=(x_{gc}-\hat\mu_{gc})/\sqrt{\hat\mu_{gc}+\hat\mu_{gc}^{2}/\hat\psi_{g}}.

Cell type is left out of the fit on purpose. The count models of Section 3.3.1 fit the type effect directly, without regularising the overdispersion and without the clip.


Between/within ratio rank
The residual matrix of one slot is split by type. With C_j cells of type j, \bar r_{gj} the mean residual of gene g in type j, and v_{gj} its within-type variance, the two decompositions are

\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}C_{j}\bigl(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}\sum_{c\in j}\bigl(r_{gc}-\bar r_{gj}\bigr)^{2}
\tag{3.6}
(every cell has weight one), and

\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\bar r_{gj},
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}(\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}})^{2},
\qquad
\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
=
J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}v_{gj}
\tag{3.7}
(every type has weight 1/J). The score is the ratio of the between term to the within term.
Two global lists are built per slot (anova_ss(), anova_ms_equal_type(), rank_ratio()):

Global, equal cell weight. Top n_genes_global = 500 genes by \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}} (ranks_global.csv). The largest type dominates.
Global, equal type weight. Top 500 by \mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within}} (ranks_global_equal_type.csv). This list feeds the export of




Each list is then united with the signalling markers of the types scored in that slot (Section 3.2.2). At 48 h the leading equal-cell ratios land on naïve-pluripotency markers; at 96 h the top gene is the endoderm marker Sox17. The residual clip changes only the far tail of these ratios.

title: 4  Covariance estimation
text:
4.1 Scope and status
This chapter estimates, for each scored cell type j at each bulk-matched time, the mean \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and the within-type covariance \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of the gene panel of tier (ii) (Section 3.3), and exports them on the linear scale of DeCovarT’s convolution,
\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\succ 0 .
\tag{4.1}
The target is the covariance that enters the likelihood, not a mechanistic gene network; a dense estimate is therefore an acceptable plug-in (3.2, why a regularised covariance).
Plug-in and sensitivity analyses. The exported plug-in is the shrinkage covariance (Section 4.2.1). Four arms are sensitivity analyses of that choice: the graphical lasso (3), the SILGGM support with a refit (Section 4.2.4), PLNnetwork (Section 4.2.5) and the shrinkage of the denoised covariance (2). All five are scored by the same nested cross-validation (Section 4.3); their theory is summarised in 3.2, estimators.

4.1.1 Inputs and scales
Every arm reads the raw UMI counts of the scored cells, element slots[[time]] of output/feature_selection/tier_01/scored_slots.rds (Section 3.2.1): counts (genes × cells), cell_type, batch and library_size, the full RNA library of each cell. The 500-gene legacy export of Section 3.6 is no longer read. A transformation belongs to one arm only.
Normalisation. The exported means and covariances are computed on raw per-cell UMI counts, with no per-cell library division (normalise = "none"). Dividing each cell by its total library removes the type-level transcriptome size S_j: signatures become mRNA fractions, and the proportions are estimated as q_j\propto p_jS_j instead of p_j (Lu et al. 2025). It also removes the biological size variation between cells of one type, which the bulk accumulates. Without spike-ins the technical size factor cannot be separated from the biological one, so the size term of the covariance is bracketed by the coefficient \kappa of the denoised estimator (2): \kappa=0 treats all size variation as biological; \kappa=\hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu) treats it all as technical, which matches library normalisation for the covariance. 4.1.3 Bulk depth per cell
Which covariance enters the bulk law, raw or denoised, depends on the bulk depth per cell relative to the reference (3.2, raw or denoised): the raw covariance is exact only at a_i=1. For bulk sample i,

a_i=\frac{y_{+i}/n_i}{\bar s_{\mathrm{ref}}},
\tag{4.2}

with y_{+i} the total counts of the bulk sample, n_i the number of cells in it, and \bar s_{\mathrm{ref}} the median UMIs per reference cell at the matched time. a_i<1 is expected: the bulk library is deeper in total than one droplet, but it spreads that depth over every cell of the pooled sample. Bulk counts are reads, not UMIs, so their sampling noise is overdispersed, with a dispersion \omega_i\ge1 that lowers the effective depth to a_i/\omega_i. The raw plug-in, the implemented default, assumes a_i=1. n_i is TODO: cells per gastruloid × gastruloids per bulk sample, from the Suppinger et al. 2023 methods (Suppinger et al. 2023).

4.2.1 Shrinkage covariance
fit_cov_shrinkage() calls corpcor::cov.shrink() (Schäfer et al. 2021) with the Schäfer–Strimmer target D: variances kept, correlations shrunk towards zero by a common factor (Schäfer and Strimmer 2005). corpcor 1.6.10 also shrinks the variances towards their median by default; lambda.var = 0 switches that off, so the target is exactly D. The closed-form intensity \hat\lambda^{\ast} (corpcor::estimate.lambda()) is the centre of the grid, and cross-validation picks the value used. The estimate is positive definite for any C_j and G_t, so it is the plug-in, and the estimator used when the others fail. The theory is in 3.2, shrinkage.


4.2.2 Denoised shrinkage
fit_cov_shrinkage(preprocess = "denoised", kappa) applies the moment correction of 3.2, raw or denoised before the shrinkage. With \boldsymbol{V}_j the unbiased sample covariance of the raw counts of the C_j cells and \bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j their mean (denoise_covariance()),

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{V}}_j
=
\boldsymbol{V}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)
-\kappa\Bigl[\boldsymbol{V}_j-\operatorname{diag}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j)
+\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_j^{\top}
-\frac{\boldsymbol{V}_j}{C_j}\Bigr].
\tag{4.3}


The eigenvalues of \widetilde{\boldsymbol{V}}_j below zero are raised to zero, the nearest positive semi-definite matrix in Frobenius norm TODO-cite: Datta & Zou 2017 (CoCoLasso); Loh & Wainwright 2012; keys not in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib. This costs one eigen-decomposition of a G_t\times G_t matrix per training set.
A gene whose denoised variance is not positive is a Poisson gene at this depth. Its variance is floored at 10^{-4} times the median positive denoised variance, its correlations are set to zero, and it is listed in floored_genes.
Target D is applied to the projected matrix: \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_{j}=\boldsymbol{D}^{1/2}\{(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\}\boldsymbol{D}^{1/2}, with \boldsymbol{R} and \boldsymbol{D} its correlation and variances, and \lambda chosen on the grid of Section 4.2.1.

The exported matrix is \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_{j}. The held-out cells are raw counts and carry the Poisson noise and the size term that the correction removed, so the arm is scored through the raw count covariance rebuilt from the estimate, with \nu^{\mathrm{tech}}=\kappa/(1-\kappa):

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{score}}_{j}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_{j}
+\operatorname{diag}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j})
+\frac{\kappa}{1-\kappa}
\bigl(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_{j}
+\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\bigr)
\tag{4.4}

(reconstruct_count_covariance(), element score_sigma of the fit, used by score_fit() when present). With \kappa=0 it is \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_{j}+\operatorname{diag}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}). The cross-validation therefore compares only how the biological part is regularised; it cannot choose \kappa, because every \kappa rebuilds the same raw moments up to regularisation. \kappa stays a bracket: the nested comparison uses \kappa=0, which needs no estimate, and the upper end \hat\kappa_{\max}=\hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu) is exported as a variant (shrinkage_denoised_kappa_max), tuned but not compared.
\hat\nu comes from extrinsic_noise_nu(): the mode of the normalised covariances \widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(x_g,x_h)/(\bar x_g\bar x_h) over pairs of genes with a mean of at least one count (at most 2,000 genes, largest means first), after Fang and Pachter TODO-cite: Fang & Pachter 2025, extrinsic biological stochasticity; key fangExtrinsicBiologicalStochasticity2025 is in the DeCovarT bibliography, not in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib. The estimate assumes that most gene pairs are intrinsically uncorrelated; co-regulated modules bias \hat\nu upwards. Without spike-ins \hat\nu mixes the biological and technical size factors, so \hat\kappa_{\max} is the all-technical end of the bracket. The estimates are written per unit to output/grn/cv/extrinsic_noise.csv.
The graphical lasso and the SILGGM refit accept the same preprocessing (preprocess = "denoised"). The graphical lasso then fits the correlation of the projected matrix. For SILGGM, ranks cannot be denoised: the support still comes from the nonparanormal scores, and only the linear-scale refit on that support uses the projected matrix. Neither variant is an arm of the nested comparison.


4.2.3 Graphical lasso with an unpenalised diagonal
fit_cov_glasso() standardises the panel, fits glasso::glasso(R, rho = lambda, penalize.diagonal = FALSE) (Friedman et al. 2019) on the sample correlation \boldsymbol{R}_j by block coordinate descent (Friedman et al. 2008), and rescales: \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\Delta_j^{-1/2}\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{R}\Delta_j^{-1/2} with \Delta_j=\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{V}_j) (rescale_correlation_fit()). With the diagonal unpenalised the fitted correlation keeps a unit diagonal, so \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} matches the sample variances.

penalize.diagonal defaults to TRUE in glasso 1.11; it is set explicitly.
huge (Zhao et al. 2022) is not used: huge.glasso() always penalises the diagonal and has no switch for it (checked in the huge 1.5.1 sources). The reasons are in 3.2, graphical lasso.
Grid endpoints come from lambda_endpoints(): at \lambda_{\max}=\max_{g\neq g'}|R_{gg'}| the off-diagonal precision is zero; the lower end is of order \sqrt{\log G_t/C_j}.
A gene constant across the cells of a type is left out of that type’s fit and listed in excluded_genes, instead of forcing a diagonal covariance for all genes.
A penalty whose solve fails is dropped from the grid and listed in failed_lambda, instead of being replaced by a diagonal precision.

The earlier selector, a safeguarded EBIC interval search (ebic_adaptive_path(), at most n_solves = 40 solves, \gamma=0.5 (Foygel and Drton 2010)), is kept in scripts/03_01_grn_glasso.R as a diagnostic path. It no longer chooses \lambda.


4.2.4 SILGGM support, then a refit
fit_cov_silggm_refit() runs in three steps:

Nonparanormal scores with huge::huge.npn(x, npn.func = "shrinkage") (rank R_{gc} mapped to \Phi^{-1}\{R_{gc}/(C_j+1)\}, then standardised). The choice of shrinkage over truncation is argued in 3.2, nonparanormal.
SILGGM::SILGGM(npn, method = "D-S_GL", global = TRUE, alpha) (Zhang et al. 2018b, 2018a): de-sparsified graphical lasso with the global FDR rule of

The object kept is the support at level \alpha (global_decision), not the dense de-sparsified matrix.

An SPD refit on the linear-scale panel under the zeros of that support, with glasso::glasso(V, rho = 0, zero = ..., penalize.diagonal = FALSE); with preprocess = "denoised", on the projected denoised matrix of




The script scripts/03_02_grn_silggm.R (seed 1, \alpha=0.05) stops after step 2 and has never been run; the refit lives in the wrapper.


4.2.5 PLNnetwork
fit_cov_plnnetwork() fits the Poisson-lognormal network of PLNmodels (Chiquet et al. 2025, 2018) to the raw counts of one unit, with the full-library offset:

x_{gc}\mid\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}
\sim
\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s_{c}\,e^{z_{gc}}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{z}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}^{-1}\ \text{penalised off the diagonal}.
\tag{4.5}

\begin{algorithm} \caption{PLNnetwork: alternating graphical lasso and variational updates} \begin{algorithmic} \Require counts $X$, offsets $O=\log s$, penalty $\lambda$, weights $W$ \State initialise the variational means $M$, variances $S$ and $\Sigma$ \For{$h = 1,\ldots,$ maxit\_out} \State $\Omega^{(h)} \gets$ \Call{GraphicalLasso}{$\Sigma^{(h-1)}, \lambda W$} \State $(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)}) \gets$ \Call{NLopt}{$B^{(h-1)},M^{(h-1)},S^{(h-1)};\Omega^{(h)}$} \State $\Sigma^{(h)} \gets C^{-1}\left[{M^{(h)}}^\top M^{(h)} + \sum_c S_c^{(h)}\right]$ \State $F_h \gets -\mathrm{ELBO}(B^{(h)},M^{(h)},S^{(h)},\Omega^{(h)}) + \lambda\|\Omega^{(h)}\|_{1,W}$ \If{$|F_h-F_{h-1}|/|F_h| <$ ftol\_out} \State \textbf{break} \EndIf \EndFor \State \Return $(B,M,S,\Omega,\Sigma)$ \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Algorithm 4.1 is the block-coordinate scheme of Chiquet et al. (2018). The model, the variational bound and the role of the offset are in 3.2, PLN.
The latent moments (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}) are not on DeCovarT’s scale. Given the library s_c of a cell, the moments of its counts are

\mathbb{E}\,x_{gc}=s_{c}\,e^{\mu_{z,g}+\sigma_{z,gg}/2},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}
=
\operatorname{diag}(\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c})
+
\bigl(\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}\,\mathbb{E}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c}^{\top}\bigr)
\circ
\bigl(e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigr),
\tag{4.6}
with e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}} taken entrywise.  On raw counts (normalise = "none"), pln_linear_moments(scale = "counts") averages Equation 4.6 over the libraries of the cells being scored, by the law of total covariance:

\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}=\bar s\,\boldsymbol{m},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\boldsymbol{x}
=
\bar s\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{m})
+\overline{s^{2}}\,(\boldsymbol{m}\boldsymbol{m}^{\top})
\circ\bigl(e^{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigr)
+\operatorname{Var}(s)\,\boldsymbol{m}\boldsymbol{m}^{\top},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{m}=e^{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z}+\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z})/2},
\tag{4.7}

with \bar s, \overline{s^{2}} and \operatorname{Var}(s) the mean, mean square and variance of those libraries. This is the matrix that is scored, comparable with the raw sample covariance. The offset removes every size variation from \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}, biological size included, so PLNnetwork needs no moment correction, only a choice of what to put back at export. Beside the scored moments, the driver exports the two brackets without the Poisson diagonal (poisson_diag = FALSE): \kappa=0 keeps the depth terms (size_term = "keep"), and the all-technical end gives every cell the mean library, so \operatorname{Var}(s)=0 and \overline{s^{2}}=\bar s^{2} (size_term = "drop"). With normalise = "library" the moments are divided by the size factor instead (scale = "normalised").

title: 4  Covariance estimation
text:
4.3 Cross-validation and outputs
The same loss selects the tuning parameter of every arm and compares the five: the held-out Gaussian log-likelihood on the linear scale. For held-out cells \mathcal{T} and an estimate (\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) fitted without them,

\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}};\mathcal{T})
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{T}}
\log\phi_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c};\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\bigr),
\tag{4.8}
computed by heldout_gaussian_logscore() through a Cholesky factor of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}; for the denoised arm, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} is Equation 4.4. Why this score is a legitimate loss for the covariance even though cells are not Gaussian is in 3.2, Gaussian log-score, and why it replaces AIC, BIC and EBIC as the selector in 3.2, cross-validation.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Tuning by K-fold cross-validation, and nested comparison of the five arms} \begin{algorithmic} \Procedure{CVSelect}{$X, f, \Lambda, K$} \State split the cells of $X$ into $K$ folds at random, with a fixed seed \For{$\lambda \in \Lambda$} \For{$k = 1,\ldots,K$} \State $(\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma) \gets f(X_{-k};\lambda)$ \State $\ell_k(\lambda) \gets$ \Call{HeldOutLogScore}{$\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma,X_k$} \EndFor \State $m(\lambda) \gets$ mean of $\ell_k(\lambda)$; $\mathrm{se}(\lambda) \gets$ its standard error \EndFor \State $\lambda_{\min} \gets \arg\max_{\lambda} m(\lambda)$ \State $\lambda_{1\mathrm{se}} \gets$ most regularised $\lambda$ with $m(\lambda) \ge m(\lambda_{\min}) - \mathrm{se}(\lambda_{\min})$ \State \Return $(m, \mathrm{se}, \lambda_{\min}, \lambda_{1\mathrm{se}})$ \EndProcedure \Procedure{NestedCompare}{$X, \{(f_e,\Lambda_e)\}_{e=1}^{5}, K_{\mathrm{out}}, K_{\mathrm{in}}$} \For{$k = 1,\ldots,K_{\mathrm{out}}$} \For{$e = 1,\ldots,5$} \State $\lambda_e \gets \lambda_{\min}$ of \Call{CVSelect}{$X_{-k}, f_e, \Lambda_e, K_{\mathrm{in}}$} \State $(\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma) \gets f_e(X_{-k};\lambda_e)$ \State $s_{ek} \gets$ \Call{HeldOutLogScore}{$\hat\mu,\hat\Sigma,X_k$} \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $(s_{ek})$, paired by outer fold \EndProcedure \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Settings in scripts/03_04_cv_covariance.R:

cv_select_tuning(X, fit_fun, grid, K = 5, seed) returns the mean and standard error per grid value and the min and 1se choices. The exported fit uses min; 1se is reported beside it.
nested_cv_compare(X, estimators, K_outer = 5, K_inner = 5, seed) is run only to compare the five arms. The inner loop chooses the tuning parameter, the outer loop scores the chosen fit on cells it never saw. The denoised arm enters with \kappa=0; the \hat\kappa_{\max} variant is tuned by cv_select_tuning() alone (2).
Folds split cells of one unit. The score measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not to new specimens (Note 3.1).
In units with very few cells (29 cells for the somite differentiation front, against 5,821 panel genes) each training fold has about 23 cells; the shrinkage estimate is the only one expected to be stable there.
Run time. At 96 h the panel has 5,821 genes. SILGGM (D-S_GL) then tests about 1.7\times10^{7} gene pairs per unit and PLNnetwork updates a 5{,}821\times5{,}821 latent covariance at every step, each refitted K times for selection and K_{\mathrm{out}}(K_{\mathrm{in}}+1) times for the comparison; these two arms dominate the cost. No cap on the panel is imposed to save time.

Diagnostics that are computed but do not select. The held-out log-score of Equation 4.8 is the only selector. The diagnostics of 3.2, diagnostics describe a fit; none of them chooses a tuning value or an arm.

For every arm: the condition number and the eigen-spectrum of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} against the Marchenko–Pastur band of the sample covariance TODO-cite: Marchenko & Pastur 1967; key not in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib; the bootstrap spread of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} in Frobenius and Bures distance (Section 4.3.2); and the Hellinger distance and MixSim overlap between types (Melnykov et al. 2012) (4). Only the last two are coded (gaussian_hellinger(), gaussian_mixsim_overlap()); the spectrum and the bootstrap spread are planned.
For the sparse arms only: EBIC along the graphical-lasso path

and edge stability under subsampling. Both count edges, so they do not apply to the shrinkage arms. StARS (Liu et al. 2010) is not run: with 20 subsamples and 40 penalties it costs about 800 graphical-lasso solves per unit, against 40 for the EBIC path.



For the arm retained for a unit, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} is the mean of the raw counts of its cells and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} is the selected covariance, both on the scale of Section 4.1.1; Equation 4.1 holds by construction. For PLNnetwork both come from Equation 4.7; for the denoised arm the exported covariance is \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{\mathrm{bio}}_{j}. Which covariance layer these cell-level moments identify, and how the sample scales are estimated inside the DeCovarT fit, is in 2.1, three regimes and 2.1, profile Newton.


4.3.1 Displays
Plot functions are in R/plot_grn_regularisation.R. Each display answers one question.
Choosing the tuning parameter (one unit, one arm).

Cross-validation curve: m(\lambda)\pm\mathrm{se}(\lambda) against the tuning parameter, with the min and 1se choices marked (new; not produced yet).
Regularisation path: each off-diagonal entry of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}(\lambda) against \log\lambda, five edges that survive at the selected \lambda and five that are driven to zero (graphical lasso, PLNnetwork).
EBIC against \log\lambda, and EBIC against edge density |E|/\{G(G-1)/2\} (diagnostic only).

Comparing arms (one unit).

Outer-fold held-out scores s_{ek} of Algorithm 4.2, one line per fold across the five arms, so that the comparison is paired.
Partial-correlation heatmaps at the selected tuning parameter, with one gene order frozen across estimators and types, 
\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}
=
-\frac{\omega_{gg'}}{\sqrt{\omega_{gg}\omega_{g'g'}}},
\tag{4.9} on a diverging scale centred at zero.
For the three sparse estimators: UpSet plots of edge presence and of signed edges.

Comparing types (one time). Pairwise Hellinger distance and MixSim overlap between the exported Gaussians on the linear scale (gaussian_hellinger(), gaussian_mixsim_overlap() in R/ebic_regularisation_path.R). Distances computed on another scale (nonparanormal scores, \log(1+x)) do not describe what DeCovarT has to separate.


4.3.2 Evaluation
There is no ground-truth network for murine gastruloids, and the estimand is a covariance. The scores are therefore relative, in this order of weight:

Held-out likelihood, outer folds of Algorithm 4.2: the selector, and the only score that compares all five arms on one scale.
Downstream deconvolution: DeCovarT error on the matched 48 h bulk and in the misspecification sweep of Section 7.1, with \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} from each arm. This is the score tied to the paper’s estimand.
Technical stability: a bootstrap of cells within type, labels fixed (Note 3.1). Edge-inclusion frequencies for the sparse estimators and the Frobenius spread of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} for every arm. Conditional on this specimen.
Separation of types: Hellinger and MixSim overlap of



Concordance of the sparse estimators: overlap of edge sets (intersection over the smaller set) and Hamming distance between skeletons, raw and divided by G(G-1)/2. Agreement is a robustness number, not a validation.

Scores that need a known skeleton, curated transcription-factor targets, other assays or perturbations are perspectives (3.2, perspectives).

title: 5  Applying and comparing deconvolution outputs applied to Suppinger study
text:
5.1 What is being compared
DeCovarT deconvolves bulk profiles with both a mean signature and a per-type covariance. Every method below uses the same gene panel and the same labelled single-cell reference; they differ in what they model beyond the mean. All runs are planned on GSE229386, at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, for the standard Wnt pulse and the early pulse (Section 2.1). Each model is reviewed in 5.1, review; one line here says what it models and how it is called.
